Just what have you seen of that transition and was it important to keep the Troy Mason pairing together? >> You know, at at first I when we were talking about it, um Mason has probably close to 2,800 3,000 reps at left guard in college. So his transition was pretty easy and he's been playing in consecutive games where Troy had the hiccup there when he was injured. Um and then then of course when you move over there he says oh you kept him together. Well I think that you know that was like a not an afterthought but it was a thought like oh okay well that's fine too because communication and those things are very important. Um, but I can tell you when you go to the left side or right side, the communication, um, just like we're having here, you're on my right and I know this. So, my head turns, my body language and all those things apply. So, now they're working inside out because now he's on his left. So, it is different and it's different even for a center and a right guard. It's different. You have it takes time and it's and you have to be adaptable and adjustable and they they are that. With that in mind, how important is it for them to be here in these early stages to work on those little micro movements before you get into treating care? >> Oh, it's it you it's it's big. It really is. I mean, you know, we use the term huge and all that. It's it's not it doesn't define everything, but it it allows you to take other steps and to see how um players can adapt to each other and to the system. So, it is it is big to say there, right? employ a extra tackle tight end type guy in the running game similar to what Anderson did here last year or is that what the fullback's for? >> Um well we have a fullback now so um you know we haven't gotten that far into that uh to be completely transparent with you. Um we've got base downs and those type of things. So those will come come at a later time. >> That's kind of a skill, right? Not every lineman can >> Oh no, no. That's You're darn right it is. It's when you get on the edge there and you start playing around and getting expanded uh formations and you have to motion motion across insert schemes. It's you have to have the right person. >> What does two more guys you guys have been excited about how he's what he's how he started with you guys as far as you know we talk about how he's raw from college but it seems like he's a very he is a smart player with a lot of footwork. >> Oh yes he is. He's very smart and um you know he's coming in and he has the luxury of having good players in front of him. so he doesn't have to start from square one and I think that's always a bonus for a younger player but um his athleticism that we saw on tape and um and all that stuff is is is what it is and he's uh he's a very good athlete and um hey he's going to accelerate like you know when these tack these young tackles have really good rushers um had a kid David Bakiari at Green Bay and he had to rush against Clay Matthews uh he had Julius Peppers. I mean, when you have this type of variation and having it here with these ex these guys are extremely productive rushers. Uh different body types, different styles, it only accelerates the edge players and so training camp will be very big for him. >> What do you think you want to see the run game develop? And how do you see Rico and Jaylen Warren fitting within that? They interchangeable or are they specific role guys? Uh, you know, that's not my position, so I won't talk about them um as players, but they're both very good football players. Uh, run game is is a big part of the offense of Coach McCarthy's, and um, we have to be able to run the football to be effective. There's so many things come off of that and that always is a starting point. So, >> where do you think Broadick will fit in when he gets back? >> He'll play tackle. you know, obviously he'll be a tackle and uh just hoping that, you know, he needs to get healthy and and he's doing what he can now and he does participate when, you know, with with all the doctor rules and those things. So, um we're just, you know, excited to have him and get him back and when he's ready then, uh that's another piece of the puzzle. That's a that's a good football play. >> Thanks, guys. >> What is it that you see from M? How intricate is he? How detailed is he when working with those guys? >> Oh, it's incredible. um you know working with with coach McCarthy um you know really you know it's a blessing for me as a as a quarterback coach and you know someone who played the position and you know just the level of thought that he puts in you know to that to that group and you know really it starts with you know how we do everything you know in our organization. It always starts with how is this going to affect the quarterback? How is this going to impact the quarterback and his development and all those things. So everything that we do kind of starts with, you know, with that premise is how do we make the quarterback successful? And the level of detail that goes into to coaching the position, um, you know, to coaching, you know, the offensive system, um, I think is is really unique and, you know, it's it's certainly helped benefit, you know, each of the quarterbacks in our room and, you know, it's helped me as a coach as well, you know, just being able to coach to those details. >> Was it eye opening for you? you know, I I don't know if it was totally eye openening because I did have, you know, experience with coach um you know, in Green Bay, his his first year there in 2006. Um, you know, spent the whole offseason there and I I've I've said this to, you know, to the quarterbacks in the past before obviously coach was here and just I've always shared that experience and, you know, that was really, you know, it was really a game changer for me. I learned so much about playing the position. um I became a better player um you know through it and you know it's it's impacted me as a coach you know forever. I've coached in that way um you know from from what I learned from coach McCarthy back in 2006 ever since. So um you know I wouldn't say it's eye opening um but you know it's exciting because everything that you know I was kind of telling these guys about my experience now they're you know having an opportunity to go through that you know themselves. Speaking of experience, um, you know, Mike McCarthy's talked a lot about the QB school. Having gone through that yourself, >> what what are some of the central components of that? What are some of the key parts and how how is that beneficial for a quarterback? >> Well, I'll tell you the most important thing is the time devoted to the quarterback training. Um, you know, and again, it goes back to how the schedule is set up and, you know, obviously all well within the the rules of the of the CBA and and all of those things, but we have ample amount of time to train and develop the quarterbacks. Um, and I think that that's the most important thing. Um, you know, there's a there's a lot of great coaches in the NFL and everybody's coaching the quarterbacks at a high level. Um, you know, in in this league. Um, but I don't think that everybody has the same amount of time um to do that work. and you know coaches you know makes it a priority in in our schedule. Um you know and we have the ability to to really you know train the footwork to train um you know all the different drills and the concepts and the different types of throws um you know that we're asking these guys to make. Um so it's pretty you know pretty unique in that way. >> How much have you seen that quarterback school evolve? I mean I assume you went through it back in in 2006. How much has it changed from that original version to what it is now? >> That that was what I was really excited to see like the evolution of it and really within the new rules um you know how how is it implemented because um you know when I went through it I think you know I don't I feel like we reported sometime in midFebruary and you know we were there we were lifting weights at like 7:00 in the morning. Um we'd have quarterback meetings from 8:30 till you know 11:00. We'd be on the field from come back, have meetings from like 1 to 3:30. Um, and I'm like, how are we going to do all of that with, you know, with the current rules. Um, but you know, seeing again, you know, the way the way this the schedule is structured, um, you know, to to make the most of that time, obviously, we don't have, you know, the same amount of hours and, you know, to to do it. But, um, you know, it's again, like that was, you know, was was really interesting for me to see. But in terms of the fundamentals of it, it's all very similar. It's all, you know, what I remember. Um, and you know, it's time tested, you know, and it's proven, you know, and it's obviously, you know, the, you know, the star players that, you know, the coaches had the opportunity to work with and and help develop and, you know, and Brett and Aaron and Dak. Um, but you think about some of the backups um that played exceptionally well in their opportunities to start for extended periods of time. I mean, most recently, I mean, you look at Cooper Rush, you know, with the Cowboys, you know, somebody who obviously went through the quarterback school and um, you know, obviously the guys, you know, all the different backups in Green Bay that had opportunities to play um, you know, for extended periods. um you know it's it's pretty it's pretty remarkable and there's you know definitely um you know there's there's you know it's a proven you know methodology and uh we're certainly seeing it in our guys in the short amount of time u that we've been working with them there's there's been a big improvement um you know in a number of different areas >> I think Mike talked about doing video profiles of every player did he do a video profile of you have you watched >> Yeah he did uh actually um the first day when we introduced the profile and kind of talked about it with the quarterbacks um he had put together and he went back and found uh you know found some clips from from my first profile and you know and showed you know kind of put it up there as an example. Um, so yeah, it was fun to to go back through that and again I I look at, you know, we do it a couple times in the offseason, you know, do it right at the beginning of the offseason, do it again at the end. And looking at who I was, the quarterback I was fundamentally from the first profile to the second profile, I mean, it's you look like a completely different person. Um, and you know, we're we're kind of feeling that now. And I think, you know, certainly it's still pretty early for Drew, but you know, Mason and Will who have been, you know, in it, you know, since, you know, since the beginning of the offseason program, um, I mean, they look they look fantastic. I mean, they're they're doing they're doing a great job and and really developing through that program. >> What is different with Will this year? >> Um, you know, I don't know if anything's different. Um, you know, I think, you know, Will, um, Will's Will, you know, in the sense of, you know, he's really smart. Um, he's a hard worker, he's competitive. Um, you know, you're seeing all of those same things. And I think for him, um, you know, what's been been really good is just, you know, the the level of detail in the preparation and the training. um you know I think has allowed him a player like you know of his caliber from a mental standpoint and his ability to to process information and and utilize that information um I think is really beneficial for him and really helpful for him and obviously he's performed well here and you know in OTAAS up to this point but um you know I mean once we get to training camp and get into preseason I think that's where you know that's where the the true evaluation will start to to take place but he's he's doing everything and more um that we could ask of him. He's exceeding expectations. Um so we, you know, couldn't be couldn't be happier with where he's at. >> What's the biggest challenge of focusing on two young quarterbacks, developing them at different paces and how you kind of streamline a process to work with? >> Yeah, it's it's interesting. Um you know, and I think it's really good. I think it's really positive to have two young guys together. Um obviously a little bit different stages and, you know, different players. Um, but two guys that are going to be very competitive with one another. You know, they get along well. They're both great, great people. Um, smart uh players. Um, but they're, you know, they're ultra competitors. They wouldn't be here um, you know, if they weren't. So, you know, just I'm very excited to see how that continues to to play out as as we get into training camp, as we get into the preseason. um you know just how the two of them bring the best out in each other because I think ultimately that's that's what our goal is is to bring the best out you know in each other and um you know when you're when you're looking at it from a a competitive standpoint like that's you know you always respect the person who's who you're competing with because they bring out the best in you and I think that will and and Drew will certainly have that you know that type of relationship and um you know it's exciting for us as coaches to you know to look forward to watching that all unfold >> kind of on two more guys, four quarterbacks, all with very different experience levels and probably different needs because of that. How does that impact your job to make sure that each guy is getting what they need out of you? >> Yeah, it's a that's a great question and and certainly a challenge. And I think that, you know, in my time here in Pittsburgh, it's it's really been that way. I mean, I think about my first year that room with uh you know, with Russell Wilson, Justin Fields, Kyle, Kyle Allen. Um, you know, three guys at very different points in their career and different, you know, different things to prove, you know, particularly with Russell and Justin. Um, and you know, we had to adapt how we coach, you know, the group together to to bring out the best in each of them. And I think that, you know, we have that now. You know, you have Aaron who's what is this 22 years uh for Aaron. Mason's heading into his ninth season. Will iss going into year two, but you know, didn't get to do a whole lot dealing with injuries um you know, last year. So, it's almost like a year one, you know, for him. And Drew is a rookie. So, you have, you know, these different level of experiences, different um you know, and I think that they're able to help each other number one, you know, first and foremost. Aaron is incredible uh with the entire group, especially with Will and and Drew as young players. Um but even Mason, I mean, Mason's had an incredible career. Um you know, I mean, played almost a decade of football. I mean, that's pretty rare and and pretty special. So, he has some great experiences and um those guys have an opportunity to learn, you know, from him as well. So, um you know, it's it's certainly a challenge, but I think it probably benefits us more than it, you know, than it challenges us to be honest. What do you think is going to be the most notable difference about this offense with the change in? >> You know, I think it's it's probably a little early to say. I think we're still, you know, figuring out exactly who we are. Certainly, we have a playbook that we put together um you know, for the guys, you know, as they came into the offseason program. Um but that playbook is brought to life by, you know, the the the the skill set and the talents and the abilities of of each player in our offense. So, I think that's what we're going through now in OTAAS and ultimately in training camp is to determine exactly who we are and, you know, what our strengths are and um, you know, what we're going to hang our hat on. So, um, you know, to say, you know, what's going to be, you know, different, you know, I don't know yet at this point. Um, you know, but I do feel like we have a really good group. I think we have a really talented group. Um, you know, certainly our our our young offensive line has become more experienced. they've played, you know, a decent amount of football together. Um, we're really excited about them and, um, you know, the the the skill group that, you know, that that we've had that have been that have been here. And then the guys that are new, whether they're, you know, draft picks or, you know, the free agents that we've brought in, I think it's a really exciting group to coach. We feel great about them and um, you know, looking forward to, you know, to what they can accomplish together. >> Two big backs, but they've shown the ability to take it to the house. unusual for such bigger guys? >> No, definitely not. I mean, this day and age, right, you got defensive ends, I mean, running four threes and four fours, right? And so, these are two um strong, stout running backs in um in Rico and Jaylen where, you know, we're just appreciative that they have so many dynamic abilities to be able to change directions on a dime, you know, have the top end speed and and make plays. >> J said that he uh he likes the intent of the run game. You use that word specifically. >> Yeah. What do you if you hear that word, what does intent mean to you? >> Yeah, I think it's just it comes down to the intentionality that coach uh has uh coach McCarthy in regards to just delivering the um overall uh identity of the offense of the run game, how we're going to utilize those guys, you know, how we're going to, you know, one of his big things that he likes to hit is 55 completes and touches, you know, and so the run game is going to be a valuable uh piece of that. And so just his intentionality and making sure that he paints the picture for those guys along with coach Brian Angelico of just what the vision is for the offense especially in the run game. >> How do you use your experience as an offensive line coach to coach the running backs cuz obviously the running game can be you know those two like Naji Harris used to spend time in the offensive line meeting rooms like how do you use that experience to help coach the running back? Yeah, definitely. It's all about collaboration, right? Just getting on the same page with coach coach camping. Um, you know, teaching the running backs that, you know, it's our job to be the grit and the glue uh for the offensive line, right? Um, build the um relationship with them, understand how they work their singles, their doubles, and things of that nature. And I can kind of help them visualize what the intent of behind the play, not just running lines on paper, but also, you know, actually understanding what our objective is and how we're going to remove and displace the black dot. And so it's just a collaboration piece. Um, you know, starting with the running backs, but also just building a relationship with the offensive line. So, it's going great. >> That was very important for him at Iowa. You know, he didn't have the best year last year, but where have you guys seen his development as far as where his head's at and what you guys are able to ask him right now? >> Yeah, I mean, with Caleb, the number one thing is just his professionalism. He's taken that to another level. He's been he's been doing a great job uh from his body of work, showing up every day, you know, doing the little things, studying, uh building a relationship with the guys in the room, leaning on guys like Rico and Jaylen, and um just making himself as accessible as he possibly can so that he can continue to grow. >> In terms of dividing the labor, do you envision a first and second down back and then a third down guy or will it be more particularly with Warren and Dow will be more your series, your series all the time? >> Yeah, definitely. No, that's a great question. it um per game it will define itself right what scheme we're going to um highlight you know what scheme we're going to um you know basically star in that game or things of that nature but when it comes to Jaylen and Rico like coach will define that you know he wants two fresh backs at all time right and so we'll find ways to make sure that we get them on the field and they have ample amount of equal time on the field um but it'll it'll define itself by scheme by game plan >> that 55 you're talking about obviously you had experience with Mike in Dallas. Was that always been a talking point of getting to that 55 number? >> Yeah, coach is a numbers guy, man. He's he's he's t he's dialed in and he's in tune to statistics and numbers and making sure that he's spreading the ball around and he's getting all players engaged. So, that's one big thing with >> No matter how you get to the 55, >> hey, what whatever his vision is, we'll follow it. >> How do you see the fullback impacting your role? >> Um, Riley's been doing a great job. You know, he's been spending more time with coach Robert Cougler, right? right now we've been working more red zone situational football and so he's been servicing the tight end room and he has been than the uh running back room but he's had a lot of uh opportunity to get in at in 21 personnel you know uh display his talents as the lead blocker and stuff like that and so again going back to that first conversation about Riley like his job is to be able to service as many rooms as he possibly can and he's been doing a great job doing that. >> Back on backers is a historical drill here at the Steelers where the running backs would take on the linebackers and pass protection drills. Is that something you guys have? Has anyone mentioned that or talked about that still being a thing or is there a different way you guys want to go about that? >> Well, I will say I've definitely watched the tape on that, right? I've definitely watched the tape. I've watched Jaylen, I mean, lay the hat, you know what I'm saying? So, I'm definitely excited about it. Uh, I'm sure it may be something that we implement in Latro. Right now, we're more focused on taking care of the players bodies and things of that nature. Um, but I would love to I would love to implement that. >> Speaking of putting a hat on somebody, Travis Homer, that's something he's known for. What stuck out about him and especially the pass? Yeah, I mean Travis, he does a great job of finding ways to service the team. You know, we can't lose sight on how important special teams is, right? Just to make sure that you are accessible at all times for the team. And so, Travis does a dynamic job of just adding that special teams value as well as he's been bringing value to the running back's room, right? Just from the pass protection standpoint, um to communicating with the guys uh in the room. I mean, he's really evolving into a leader in the room as well. How how much uh have has McCarthy's offense kind of evolved since your time with him in Dallas? I'm sure that when you see the playbook, there were probably some things that were familiar, but is there anything that kind of took you by surprise being like, "Oh, this is some new stuff I wasn't expecting." >> I can definitely tell you we're getting back to the origin, right? We're getting back to the root of coach McCarthy. Um he's has a a a tremendous staff here that he surrounded himself with with guys who have been a part of his coaching journey back to New Orleans and Green Bay. And so not necessarily surprised at some of the things that we're uh implementing, but I'm excited to see him because, you know, he would give us some of the backstory of uh schemes and schematics, you know, from protection to the run game in Dallas to now I'm actually getting a chance to see it being implemented. So that's that's very fun. >> What is the root of McCarthy? >> The root of coach McCarthy, man, just detail. Uh a guy who loves ball and um a guy who values the why we do things, you know, I would say that's his root. You need the players to get that. >> Of course. Of course. >> Why? >> Yeah. Of course. You want the players to understand the why because at the end of the day, um the better knowledge and understanding that they have in the scheme that we're asking them to implement and to go out and and to execute, the better they perform. >> All right. Thanks a lot. >> Oh, go ahead, Jeff. >> Sorry. >> Eli, how much is he working in your room? Is he a guy like Homer that can do a lot of lot of different things eventually? >> Yeah, definitely. Eli's been in my room every day. Um, and he is a Swiss Navy knife, right? He's a Swiss Navy knife. I told him to patent that. Okay. Um, great kid. Um, um, does a great job of just meshing with the guys, the relationships, but also taking time to learn the scheme, identifying where he fits. I mean, he's been awesome for us.

title: Defensive Coaches Media Availability (May 27) | Pittsburgh Steelers
text: when you when you come into a new place, what's the process of familiarizing yourself with the personnel and then figuring out how the different skill sets might fit into what you want to do? >> Yeah, that's the first thing we do. Um sat down with with PG and wanted to know exactly how he wanted to utilize the the men at each position and and we have what we call profiles of of every player. And so we we created those and then we looked at the players that we had and who fit those profiles and the players that we needed to add to that. And so, um, we have a in the secondary a group of guys that we feel happy with and now we just have to make sure we put the right combination out there together. >> Joe, do you think you have a lot of versatility where you can do a lot of different things with the guys you have? >> We do. You know, um, the the skill sets that we have, uh, guys from both outside at corner and at at at the safety position, they can play the the star position, they can play the money position. So, um, it gives PG, Jason, and myself opportunity to to put the people in the best spots to give us a chance to win that individual game that we're that we're facing that week. And then the next week you might see a diff different grouping of guys because we're just trying to win that game. >> Start and one of your new phrases around here. >> Uh the star is the nickel and the money is the third down will type position. >> How much will Jaylen Ramsey kind of be part of those two positions? >> You know, his skill set lends himself to doing that. you know, he um I'm not going to really compare him to a guy that I coached, but the way we use Charles Woodson in Green Bay, um he played the the star, he played corner, he played safety, he played the the money, he did those things all in some Charles could do it all in one game. Um he's one of the rare guys that could do it. Uh Jaylen has a has a similar skill set, similar size, similar speed. So, um just excited to see how we work with him and and um the the way that we use him. >> Dr. Graham talked about emphasizing communication this time of year. What's the best way to go about that in the secondary to make sure that's shorter for game day? >> Well, the the the number one thing is still a communication. It's not how we did it in Green Bay or how I did it in the Raiders or or Washington or whatever. How we do it and how we call things here. And so, uh, we're very, uh, particular about, okay, this is what we're calling this route combination. This is what we're calling this check. And don't say it's just like this from what we call it here at the Steelers last year. No, it's not. this is how we're calling it this year. This is how we're doing it. So, as long as the quicker we can get those guys on page of steeler language and how we're doing it and the way that PG wants to do it, um you know, you won't see any errors in in the back end. >> Has been in voluntary practices. >> He's been to a few. Yes. >> It's important for him though, isn't it? All this new stuff. >> I I go back to when, like I said, when when I had Wood didn't come. All right. He won defensive player of the year that year. So, I mean, it is it is what it is. I mean, this this is voluntary. Guys come when they need to. Um, when you're a vet and you're of his of his stature now, we're getting information to them. They have their iPads. We send eyes um their their installs. We texted every night. So, the information is getting to the guys that aren't here. I I guarantee you that. >> How would you describe this kind of chase for the two 2010 Packers? It's kind of similar, wouldn't you say? Ask that again. >> Well, you've got Aaron by you >> and your version of Charles Woodson. It's like >> No, this is we're worried about the 2026 Steelers. That's the that's the only thing we're worried about. Everything 16 years ago, that was a total different situation. U we have we have a um opportunity to to set our mark here and that's what we want to do. We want to we just want to make the uh the Steelers the the the best that we can in 2026. and we understand what the goal is and now we just have to work extremely hard to get there. >> We've seen a >> around the league we've seen a lot of bigger nickels kind of come about where usually you I think you thought under size but now it's become even bigger nickels and Jaylen obviously fits into that. How does that modernization of that position kind of fit into your guys' vision and how does Jaylen specifically fit into that as a bigger >> Well, what people started to do, you know, you you had smaller nickels because you had quicker shift to your guys inside. So what did people start doing? and they've started putting bigger bodies on those smaller guys. So, conversely, you had to put a bigger body on him. And so, but Jaylen, he's quick enough to match some of the smaller bodies and he's big enough to defend some of the the the larger bodies. So, he's um he's a guy that, like I said, we talk about weaponizing certain players. Um him, TJ, uh Peyton, you know, just guys that we want to weaponize. He's one of the guys that we we really want to use as a weapon. when you with Woodson, does it go beyond physical traits? Is there a football IQ associated with that or >> I think so. You know, it's still early in the process with him. You know, I was I was with Wood for a long time. So, you know, like I said, I don't like to compare a lot of people to him, but they are friends and he called Wood as soon as he knew I was getting coming here cuz he knew I coached Wood. So, um but I I haven't been around him enough to know that is he as, you know, smart as Wood is when it comes to picking up things. I just I couldn't tell you that right But it was way beyond physical with Woodson, right? >> Yeah. So, what what is when you're a multi-positional player and you have to understand the scheme and what's going on around you, not just at your position, but at the positions around you because the very next play, you could be playing the star to the to the will, which is the opposite of what you just did. Uh you have to be very very smart to be able to do that. >> You talked about weaponizing your role uh and being able the assistant head coach part of your role. How does that play in? And how does having a guy who's another guy who's been a defensive coordinator on the staff, how do you see that as helping out for PG? >> I think, you know, my role is and just what you said is to help and assist Mike. All right. With the opportunity, the times that that he might not be able to run the team meeting, you know, I've been with him so long, I understand how he wants things done. All right. So, I go in there and I run the team meetings and what have you from that standpoint. PG, you know, uh to assist him, to assist Jason Simmons. That's that's my role with this this team is to make sure that um if I do my job, that means Mike's doing a hell of a job and PG and Jason, everybody's doing a hell of a job from that standpoint because I'm here to help and help the players, help the coaches, and um you know, we all work together in different facets before. And so, but that's that's what it is with the assistant head coach, you know, title. >> What you like being back here? >> Oh, I'm excited. Come on, man. You get a chance to come back to Pittsburgh. It all started here for me in 1998. I know I'm dating myself by saying that, but spending four years here. It was amazing. It kind of built my career in terms of what I became as a player and then a coach. Actually, the love of the game and being back is special. Just loving the people of Pittsburgh. >> Was there anything specific that that happened here that turned you into a coach? >> What it did though, it uh I tell you with the veteran the veteran leadership when I was here was unbelievable. You talk about guys like even on the offensive side, Vettice and Levon Kirkland on defense and Lake and Darren Perry and all of the veterans just helps you understand the structure of defense and how it was put together and what everybody did along with all the great coaches that we had here. Well, you were part of that 34 defense that Cow and Don Capers installed and Mike talks McCarthy talks about wanting to he embraces that and wants to kind of emulate that if you can. Of course, what are the keys to that 304 you see and can you see trying to maybe try to replicate that area? >> The keys to it are the people, you know, there's there's no secret the secret sauce are the players. We know it and we understand it. You put the best players in the position to make plays. You know, you have those outside linebackers. When we have multiple guys that can make plays, they have the ability to rush. They have ability to drop. That allows you to be multiple as BG will be as a as a D coordinator. >> Those outside backers though, the key to the 30 point. >> The players are always the key. It's just not the outside backers. It's also that front as well. You know, forever. They've always had like the best tackles here as well. >> So, you just talk about those those key pieces and we have those elements to play, you know, good defense here. Jason, anything about being here early in your career? You mentioned loving the game. Is it just being around those guys you mentioned or was there something about here that >> Well, it's just it's it's the building because when I talk about that, you talk about the people in the building. There's still people in the building from the cafeteria to the secretaries to the front office. People that are still people. They're all about like everybody in that building play with one scoreboard. You know, everybody's playing, everybody's on the same page, and it's all about winning. Jason, is it too person? >> Once again, it it lets me know how old I am, you know, for uh you know, even even talking to Joey, you know, I'm excited. I know he's excited. I I know that that young Joe is excited. Uh you know, having a relationship with him, knowing who he is as an athlete, as a player, uh just adding even more consistency to who he is. He's already a good player and we're just going to just continue to grow. >> Dr. Graham has told us a lot about wanting to preach the tradition here with the Steelers defense steel curtain. With your experience here, what's your role in sort of also passing along that tradition, knowing what it takes to have a great defense here? >> My role in passing on the tradition is kind of funny as that. It it's it's about keeping football first. That's that's what this place is. It's not about the glitz and the glamour. It's about ball. It's about competing. It's about communication. It's about accountability and keeping that first. That That's my part of this tradition. Have you seen that identity in the guys that you have in the building? Just getting to know them. Is that something that that you've taken from guys like Hayward and and some of those guys that have been around here a long time? Are they helping continue that tradition? >> They they absolutely are. When you when you have that type of leadership, you have that type when you have the unselfishness from guys at the top, you know, guys that have been here uh well over a decade and they embrace being here in OTAAS. They embrace the brotherhood and forming a new brotherhood and starting it every year. That can only help you. and a young guy see it. >> One of the sort of generation of players where slot quarterback was a sort of a full-time job for the first time. Uh it's now evolved way beyond that to where some defense those guys are the star player. How do you watch that happen? And how's that your experience there sort of shaped way you've implemented those guys? >> Well, as football has evolved, you know, of course, when I first started, we had 21 personnel. You everybody playing with a fullback. You don't have many teams that even have a fullback on the roster now. and just knowing the way the offense that involved and 11 personnel and having three receivers and now looking to throw the ball, you just see how much the landscape of receivers getting paid. So now that slot quarterback is a starter. So we we we embrace it and we know that's what it is and you know that's why good players play that. >> Anytime someone glitches out of the slot, someone around here might say that's Mike Hilton and I say I think Simmons. >> Were you were you innovative in that way? >> No, I was not. No, I was not. >> I didn't know. Was that happening? >> It It was It was But the thing about me is the thing that that I feel like I can bring to this group is knowing your role and knowing who you are and embracing your role. I think that's what allowed me to play 10 years in this league. It wasn't athleticism. Uh it wasn't stature. It wasn't any of those things. It was knowing your role, embracing your role, and then being able to make the people around you better if you're not the star. Joe talked about Jaylen, you know, he preparing he's number Charles Woodson when they were together in Green Bay. What does Jayen bring to the table that that helps him be that versatile weapon that you guys want to move across your defense and sign all these different? >> Well, number one, when when you talk about Draymond Ramy, you say that he's a defensive back. You know what I'm saying? He's a corner, a safety, a star. Uh you don't say that he's he's a dime. Like this guy has the ability to play on all levels on the first, second, and third level from blitzing to playing the deep ball. Uh, and Patrick is gonna utilize that. We gonna put him in the best place to make plays and really kind of make sure that this guy is used and he's out there able to make plays. >> What is the division of labor between you and Joe in terms of safeties? Is it corner safeties or do you guys collaborate in terms of position coaching in terms of secondary defensive backs? Coach, >> once again, we are defensive back coaches. You know, the the beauty of it is uh I've ran the room, Joe's ran the room, Joe's been a coordinator. The deal is we are trying to put all of that information and just give it to the players. Uh I think that the way we don't minimize them, the way we don't minimize ourselves and say corners and safeties. What we bring to the table is making sure that we raise the level so everybody understands the entire structure of the defense. >> Where do you see Joey in his career right now? I mean last year finished pretty strong with solid coverage numbers, decreased the penalties. Where do you guys see him as far as his next step as being an outside quarterback? Well, everybody here in this um everybody knows the talent that this guy is. He's an elite player in the International Football League. Uh we know it, we understand it, and anytime anytime you have a young player with that type of talent, what you want to do is focus on the consistency of it and make sure there are no lows and no ups and downs. And that's what we're here to do. >> You start to really familiarize yourself with the safety of right now with uh Elliot and also Juan Brisford. What stands out in terms of their strengths and how interchangeable might they be able to be within your the structure of your defense? >> The first thing that stands out is how coachable those guys are, how receptive they are to new information. When you have guys that have had that type of success that they both had at places that have played good defense, you know, you want to know, hey, will they receive information? And these guys are highly coachable. And the deal is they're positioning safeties. They can play down, they can play deep, they can they now can cover tight end. So they give us a lot of flexibility and I'm happy with them. You >> still close with the Shay? >> I am. >> Yeah, >> I am. I talk to DHE all the time. >> Do you guys have a battle? Who's going to be a head coach first? >> Shoot. We just try to have the best secondary first. That's where we are. >> You're not surprised he's a coach, are you? >> Not at all. >> Not at all. I mean, the shay like I told you, we were blessed to have some really, really good coaches and people to train us and people to mentor us at play. Uh, you know, he's a right. He's a brilliant mind. He's one of the best D coaches in the National Football League. We've seen a lot more defenses deploy a lot more cover four looks, you know, as far as you guys have like you see with Brian Flores in Minnesota. What do you think has caused that sort of surge, more teams wanting to do that? Is that something that you guys are excited to use defensive backs you guys have here? >> I mean, absolutely. Where the league is going to it because it allows a lot more disguise. Whenever you have that split safety shell, what are you playing out of dropping down playing single high? Are you playing cover two? Are you playing cover four? Are you playing cover zero? There are a lot of schemes that that can be employed just by playing a split safety shell. So that's why more teams are playing it >> quarterback the depth you have there. You have guys like Sante or or Brandon or a third round pick who not everybody can play I guess is what I'm saying. Is that you a you like the depth and b how they all kind of approaching that kind of fighting for roles? >> You know what of course I really like the depth. When when you're a coach we don't we don't have guys that are backups. We don't have like, hey, first group in, second group in. We realize that we have multiple starters in the secondary and we allow those guys to compete. That's what football is about. That's what Pittsburgh is about. It's about allowing those guys to compete and compete to for playing time. And as a coach, when you have four or five guys that have the ability to go out there and start, it makes your job a lot easier. >> Jason Den said last week you guys challenged him a little bit against DK. um how did he approach that challenge and how has he kind of approached the NFL game throughout his first month or so here? >> Uh when I think about him, I think about humility. Uh you know, he's played in a lot of big games coming from Georgia. Let's just be honest. That guy has played SEC championships, national championships, and he you talking about receptive to coaching. >> Yeah, he absolutely is. He is a sponge. He's a bright guy. Uh and the next thing is his poise as well to be a young guy. uh to not go up and down to realize when you say you're going against a quality receiver like DK Mechaf, he doesn't let that take him out of his technique and I love the confidence. >> You had some big time battles against this franchise. What's it been like putting on these colors? >> Oh, it's a blessing, man. You know, uh really enjoyed being here. You know what I mean? I know it's a different from when I was in Cincy and stuff like that, but I was there as a player. Now, as a coach, man, just trying to uh be the best I can and and uh be the best version of myself here. And but I'm excited, man, that the traditions, the culture, um everything I've done in the past here, it's really good to be part of it. And I just want to make my mark now, now that I'm a Steeler, uh to to continue to uh show greatness here, you know what I mean? So excited for it. >> I think uh the best way for me is daily, man. just coming in the building every day ready to work, ready to grind, and uh making my mark with the players, you know, with the guys I have in my room and the defense and just uh giving the best I can every day to to get the best out of those guys.
